FanzMAX: a Next-Generation Fanzor Genome Editor with Enhanced Editing Activity and Efficiency

Engineered Fanzor2 (Fz2) nucleases with enhanced genome editing activity in mammalian cells and demonstrated genome editing in mice.

Problem:

Protein engineering is a rapidly growing field that underpins the development of high-performance therapeutic proteins. Genome editors, such as CRISPR-based systems, have enabled precise genetic modifications and hold tremendous potential for treating genetic diseases. Despite their remarkable success, the performance of current editing platforms remains constrained by key limitations, including insufficient editing efficiency, fitness constraints, and narrow targeting scopes. Addressing these bottlenecks is critical for realizing the full therapeutic potential of engineered genome editors.

Solution:

A series of engineered Fanzor2 (Fz2) editors, termed FanzMAX, was developed through EvoMax-guided protein engineering, RNA scaffold optimization, and La protein fusion. FanzMAX v3-hLa achieved ~10-fold higher mean endogenous editing efficiency than wildtype NaloFz2 in cell-based assays and broadened the targeting scope of Fz2s. The combined engineering strategy also restored detectable activity in selected previously inactive Fz2 orthologs, and a FanzMAX v1-based construct demonstrated genome editing in mice.

Technology:

Like CRISPR-Cas systems, Fanzor nucleases are RNA-guided proteins that can be programmed to target and edit specific DNA sequences. Among them, Fanzor2 (Fz2) nucleases are compact, RNA-guided DNA endonucleases of eukaryotic origin and are well suited for delivery in a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector. Here, Fz2 orthologs were computationally identified and experimentally validated from more than 1,600 candidates. Using EvoMax, an adaptive protein engineering pipeline, together with RNA scaffold optimization and La protein fusion, Fz2 was optimized to generate FanzMAX. The resulting FanzMAX series exhibited enhanced genome editing activity in mammalian cells and demonstrated genome editing in mice, highlighting the potential of Fanzor nucleases as the next generation of genome editors.

Advantages:

  • FanzMAX v3-hLa achieved ~10-fold higher mean endogenous editing efficiency than wild-type NaloFz2 in cell-based assays 
  • FanzMAX variant demonstrated a substantially broadened genomic recognition landscape in comparison to wildtype Fz2 
  • Successful genome-editing: mice intravenously injected with AAV 1.0 carrying yLa–FanzMAX v1 achieved approximately 25% liver indel frequency at day 21 after injection




(A) Editing efficiency across eight endogenous loci by 4 different nucleases: wildtype NaloFz2, FanzMAX v3-hLa, enNlovFz2 (a different engineered Fz2 nuclease), and enCnCas12f1 (CRISPR-associated nuclease). FanzMAX v3-hLa outperformed the other tested nucleases at these loci, as measured by indel levels. (B) Schematic overview of in vivo Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV) delivery design targeting the human PCSK9 gene. Panels B–D use AAV 1.0 carrying yLa–FanzMAX v1. (C) Plasma PCSK9 levels after a single AAV dose. (D) Quantification of in vivo indel formation in liver tissue harvested on day 21 post-injection. Mice intravenously injected with this construct achieved approximately 25% liver indel frequency at day 21.
